I will explain the matter
in committee. It will take considerable time to explain it. I hope that will be satisfactory to my bon. friend. I can assure him that this drawback is a comparatively unimportant matter. That concludes the tariff changes that I have to propose in connection with the iron and steel industry.
I come now to deal with the important subject of agricultural implements, and with the consent of the House I shall treat of it somewhat at length, especially in view of the debate which took place recently upon the resolution of my hon. friend from Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles), asking for the abolition of all duties upon agricultural implements.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
when the House rose at sax o'clock, I was entering upon a consideration of the question of duties upon agricultural implements. I stated that it was my intention, to deal with the matter somewhat at length on account of the resolution which was moved by my hon. friend from Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles) in this House recently and the debate thereon which ensued. I did not take part in that debate, because, although the resolution was entirely in order, I felt that a discussion upon a matter relating to duties could more properly take place upon the occasion of the Budget Speech. Now, Mr. Speaker, it has been recognized, I think, by all governments that it is most important that duties upon agricultural implements should be fixed at rates as reasonable as possible having regard to fiscal policy. Agriculture is recognized as the great basic industry, and it is'important that the implements. which the farmer uses-his plant, so to .speak-should cost him as little as possible. This principle, Sir, is recognized in the tariff of to-day. The average rate of duty upon dutiable goods under the present tariff, the tariff of 1907-the tariff of the late Government as well as of the Government of to-day-is 26 per cent. The duties upon agricultural implements are chiefly 17i per cent and 20 per cent.
Now, there is one point to which I desire to refer in this discussion. The tariff of this or of any other country-and especially of a protective country- is a structure; one part is dependent upon another part; the rates of the tariff are related one to another; the rates on finished products are related to and largely dependent on the rates on Taw materials which are usually the finished product of other manufactures, and dutiable. This solidarity, so to speak, of the tariff cannot be lost sight of. Usually it is impossible to deal with a single item without at the same time dealing also with other related or dependent items. To arbitrarily single out special products and lower or abolish the duties upon them fwithout dealing (also with necessarily related duties would not only result in the grossest injustice to those affected thereby but would exercise a most harmful effect upon the entire industry of the nation by the ensuing loss of confidence on the part of the business community. On account of this consideration, it is unusual to make many tariff changes except upon occasions of general revision when the tariff can be dealt with as a whole after due inquiry and consideration as to the scope and bearing o.f all changes proposed. If modifications are then regarded as necessary, upon a range of products or commodities any other modifications dependent thereon or necessary thereto .may also be made, to the end that injustice and disturbance of business may, as far as possible, be avoided.
Now, Mr. Speaker, this is by way of preface to the remarks which I propose to offer in respect of the resolution which was supported, I believe, unanimously by the Liberal members of this House to the effect that:

In the opinion of this House the time has arrived when, in the interests of the farmers, and consequently in the interests of the whole of Canada, the duties on agricultural implements should be forthwith removed.
Sir, there is no reservation or exception about that resolution; it is a drastic resolution calling for the abolition of all duties upon all agricultural implements of every kind and nature whatsoever. Upon the occasion of the debate on the Address, I referred to the declaration at Hamilton and at Montreal by my right hon. friendi the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), in favour of a policy of free food, and I said on that occasion, and I say now, that free food means free trade. I say further now, that free agricultural implements means free trade.
Free trade in implements.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Free trade. Having gone so far, my right hon. friend must inevitably go farther. The logical and inevitable outcome and conclusion of his declaration respecting free food and of the policy respecting free agricultural implements is the fiscal policy of free trade. Sir, I have no exception to take to my right hon. friend espousing a policy of free trade. I simply desire to say this-that we on this side of the House are ready to accept that gage of battle, whenever he chooses to throw it down.
Now, I am going to ask this House to consider the position of the manufacturer of agricultural implements with all his duties abolished. But first, what is his position under the tariff of to-day? The manufacturer of agricultural implements, as the manufacturer of other commodities in Canada, buys subject to duty, his stone, his brick and all other building materials that enter into the composition of his establishment. He buys subject to duties his engines, his machinery and his plant generally. He pays fifty-three cents a ton upon the coal that he consumes in his furnaces. He buys subject to duty his iron, his steel, his bars, his shapes, sheets, wire, forgings, plates, nuts, washers, tubing, chains, castings and practically all other articles entering into his product. The range of duties upon the articles I have mentioned is for the most part from twenty per cent to thirty per cent. With practically everything he uses dutiable, on what principle can we sweep away the duties upon the product of the manufacturer of agricultural implements? I ask this House, upon what principle can it be done? Now, is my right hon. friend prepared to take the further logical

step and to vote for the abolition of all duties upon the raw and finished products	entering into	the manufacturing	of agricultural	implements ?
To do so would work the most serious damage to all industries concerned: to the coal industry, to our great basic iron and steel industry, to our machine and foundry industry, to say nothing of a multitude of others of minor importance. A large part of their tonnage would be lost to foreign manufacturers, and many establishments would undoubtedly close their doors. Let us assume for a moment that my right hon. friend was ready to go so far as that; would he then accomplish the end that he had in view? Could the manufacturer of agricultural implements-and by agricultural implements I mean all agricultural implements, because that is what the resolution had in contemplation-could he, if he had all the products constituting his material upon the free list, hold his own in competition with the implement makers of the United States? The cost of production is necessarily higher in Canada, even under those conditions, for this reason: it is a well-known fact that cost of production is in inverse ratio to the tonnage: the greater the tonnage, the greater the number of implements manufactured, the less the cost of production, and until this country has developed its industry to the extent to which it has been developed in the United States, it will not be possible for us to compete on even terms with the highly specialized and powerful industries of that republic.
One of the greatest markets for agricultural implements in Canada is the Northwest. I have been looking into the question of freight rates and I find that the freight rates between Chicago and Winnipeg upon agricultural implements are lower than they are between Hamilton and Winnipeg. Therefore, even if the duties upon raw materials were abolished, the Canadian manufacturer of agricultural implements would be at a disadvantage with his American competitors. That being so, what would be the inevitable result of the policy, advocated by hon. gentlemen opposite, of the abolition of duties on all agricultural implements of every kind and nature whatsoever? The effect would be this: it would transfer the entire agricultural implement business of Canada to the United States; it would depopulate some of our most thriving towns, and for what? That an American trust ultimately might gain control of the Canadian market from east to west and dictate prices at its own sweet will.

I propose to examine this agricultural implement industry; to see where are the manufactories engaged in the production of agricultural implements, and to see how important is this industry to Canada. According to the census of 1911 there are in Canada seventy-seven of these establishments, with a capital of 545,000,000. The number of employees at factories and head offices, nearly all men, is 9,560, and the amount of salaries and wages paid is *5,550,000, materials used amount to $10,400,000, and the value of products is $20,700,000. There are fifty-four of these establishments in Ontario, located at forty-three different places and in 35 electoral districts. The capital invested in Ontario alone is $44,000,000. The other establishments are located in the province of Quebec, and at Winnipeg and Brandon in the province of Manitoba. I have a complete list of the places in which there are manufactories of agricultural implements.
I shall not go through it in detail, but for the information of the House-because it was a surprise to me-I propose to mention to-night the names of the places in Canada in which agricultural implements of one kind or another are manufactured. This is The list:	Hamilton, Brockville, Toronto,
Peterborough, Preston, St. Mary's, Smith-Falls, Teeswater, Welland, Terrebonne, Guelph, Ingersoll, St. George, Woodstock, Brantford, Cowansville, Aurora, Ayr, Bolton, Goderich, Merrickville, Orillia, Paris, La Prairie, Montmagny, Tillsonburg, Brandon, Chatham, Waterloo, New Hamburg, St. Hyacinthe, Winnipeg, Ottawa, Ridgetown, St. Andre, Warwick, Summerside, P.E.I., Calgary, St. Thomas, St. Catharines, Stratford, Iberville, Joliette, Halifax, New Glasgow, Waterloo, Walkerville, Sorel, Water-ville. So far as the record goes, there are agricultural implement establishments m every province except British Columbia. In these places there is invested $45,000,000 of capital, the manufactories supporting directly, in operatives and their families, probably 50,000 people-the mainstay industrially of many of the -towns that I have mentioned, which afford .a market for the surrounding country; these .are the establishments that the policy of hon. gentlemen opposite, the policy of the .abolition, root and branch, of duties on agricultural implements, would destroy.
What is the condition to-day of those engaged in the manufacture of agricultural implements ? I have looked into this matter with a view of ascertaining the facts and dealing with them, I trust, fairly and 156
judicially. Those engaged in the manufacture of agricultural implements have felt, in common with those engaged in all other enterprises, and are feeling to-day the financial conditions which have prevailed in Canada during the past two years. Those conditions have been aggravated by a credit system under which the manufacturers of agricultural implements become virtually the bankers for many of those to whom they sell their products. Last year their expectations were , . disappointed as to the demand there would be for their productions, and to-day the agricultural implement manufacturers of Canada are carrying large inventories because of the over-production of last year. They are confronted this year with the condition that prevailed to a large extent last year. Money is becoming easier, but they do not expect that their output of this year will at all reach the output of the last and preceding years. Having regard to the fact that the tariff rates upon one commodity are fixed with regard to the rates upon the raw material entering into its production; and having regard to the financial conditions which prevail today and affect that industry in common with all others, I say that any extreme, high-handed or arbitrary action could only result most disastrously to that industry. Sir, we are not here to destroy but to encourage and promote Canadian industry.
I say that that is our mandate as a Government from the people of Canada. Now we have not been unmindful of the interests of the farmer. We have been desirous that the tariff upon his implements, his plant should be as reasonable as possible,^ consistent with our fiscal policy and conditions as they exist in Canada to-day. But, Sir, we have approached the subject in a rational way. We have . made inquiries. For considerably over a year past we have been making inquiries and investigations into the question of agricultural implements. We have made an investigation into the prices of agricultural implements on both sides of the line, in Canada and in the United States. We have made an inquiry as to the factory cost of production of the principal agricultural implements in Canada and in the United States. We have examined the balance sheets of manufacturers with the idea of ascertaining what their position is and whether or not they a -e making undue profit upon their business.

Would the hon. gentleman state whether, in making that examination, he also examined as to what amount



of cash was in the stock and what amount of water?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The examination as to
selling price was made toy a trusted official of the Customs Department, Mr. Thomas Costello. We examined into the cost of production. I examined the balance sheets myself and I think, without paying myself too much of a compliment, that I know something about a balance sheet. After having given this matter the most careful and painstaking consideration, we are satisfied that on only one range of implements can the duty be lowered without violation of the fiscal policy of reasonable protection which is designed to encourage and promote the establishment of industries in Canada. There is in the tariff an item respecting a range of implements which are much used in the northwestern provinces; I refer to harvesters, reapers, binders and mowers. I think I should point out to the House, because it is pertinent to the observations I made a short time ago with reference to the duties upon raw material entering Into products, that there exists a drawback upon iron and steel, the principal commodities used in the production of these implements, harvesters, reapers, binders and mowers. We have been asked upon more than one occasion to repeal that drawback and to give the steel manufacturers the benefit of the market. There is much to be said for that course. It is a course which would commend itself to one seeking to follow a policy of protection. But, in the interests of the farming community and having regard to the tariff as it exists to-day, we have said:	We will allow that drawback
item to stand. That drawback upon iron and steel is equivalent to about two or two and a half per cent upon the value of a binder, reaper, moweT or harvester. I differentiate the industry engaged in the manufacture of harvesters, reapers, binders and mowers from the others.
Would the minister state what he means by harvesters, reapers and binders?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am quoting the words
used in the tariff.
A harvester and a binder are the same thing, it is one machine.
Does the minister refer to two classes of machine or to one?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We will call them one, anything for peace. We will say harvesters, reapers and mowers. The binder does not 
count, because it means the same thing as a harvester. When I was a boy we used to call them binders. There are three firms in Canada engaged to-day in the manufacture of harvesters, reapers and mowers, the Massey-Harris Company, of Toronto, the International Harvester Company, of Hamilton, and the Frost & Wood Company, of Smith Falls.
And the Noxon Company, of Ingersoll.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I had overlooked that firm; I shall be glad to learn of any others. I would make this distinction between the cases of harvesters, reapers and mowers and all other agricultural implements, that for home consumption there is a drawback upon iron and steel products entering into the manufacture of those three implements. That is one point of distinction between the industries engaged in the manufacture of those implements and industries engaged in the manufacture of all other agricultural implements. Another point of distinction is this. Those are among the most highly developed industries in the world. The manufacture of harvesters, reapers and mowers has been brought to an extraordinary point of perfection both in Canada and in the United States, and it is a matter of pride to me that the Canadian manufacturer of harvesters, reapers and mowers is not only able to hold his own but to do exceptionally well and sometimes to best his competitors in the markets of the world.
Will that include corn harvesters as well* as grain harvesters?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am unable to answer that question immediately, it is a more or less technical question, and I have not the information at the moment.
They are both harvesters.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am covering, or intending to cover the item in respect of which a drawback is given on pig iron and steel and their products entering into the manufacture of the implements. I think it does include corn harvesters, but I am unable to say definitely to my hon. friend, because the matter has not been called to-my attention. What is, then, the position of these manufacturers of harvesters, reapers and mowers? The Massey-Harris Company has an export business equal to sixty-five per cent of its output. The International Harvester Company of Chicago has, of course, a laTge export

business, but I understand that its export business in Canada is not large. Having regard to the highly developed condition of this industry, and to the fact that it enjoys a drawback in respect of iron and steel, which are the principal products entering into the manufacture of agricultural implements, we have, after the most careful consideration, reached the conclusion that the duty upon harvesters, reapers, binders and mowers, which now stands at 171 per cent in the customs tariff of 1907, can ibe reduced to 121 per cent.
Why do not gentlemen opposite cheer now?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
that is 21 per cent lower than the rates upon harvesters, reapers, binders and mowers proposed in the celebrated reciprocity agreement. Having regard to the cost of production of these implements in the United States and in Canada to-day, and having regard to the greater tonnage of the United States output, and to the difference in freight rates in favour of the United States manufacturers of those implements, I say that that is as low a rate as we are able to obtain if we are to retain these great industries in the Dominion of Canada. Statistics of the Customs Department show that in respect of export of harvesters, reapers, binders and mowers, the drawback, which means all the duty that has been paid upon foreign material entering into their manufacture, is about equivalent to 5 per cent. If, therefore,- we take into consideration the 21 per cent which we are still allowing them, and, further, the 21 per cent representing the balance of that 5 per cent, harvesters, reapers, binders and mowers are really, so far as protection is concerned, on a 10 per cent basis. I have dealt, I am afraid, somewhat at length, but I hope fairly and justly, with the question of agricultural implements.
There is just one other matter that 1 have to deal with. Last year we placed upon the free list ditching machines, but inadvertently omitted parts of ditching machines. This year we shall put parts of ditching machines upon the free list.
I now come to another topic-the question of building stone. By item 306 of the tariff, there is a duty of 20 per cent on building stone dressed, and on rough stone a duty of 15 per cent. That is a difference of 5 per cent, but that margin 1561
is more than nullified by the freight rates, and for this reason: When a block of stone is dressed it loses a certain amount of its weight; dressed stone comes in at a 20 per cent duty, but in the dressing, which add* value to it, sufficient weight has been taken off the stone to more than counterbalance, having regard to freights, the-margin between the duty upon rough stone and the duty on the finished product. This has been a very great disadvantage to the-Canadian stonecutters. Notwithstanding' the building activity of the past few years, there have been frequent periods of unemployment among the stonecutters of' Canada. The stone comes from Ohio and Indiana, where, for the most part, the work is done. We have been repeatedly petitioned by the stonecutters throughout Canada for a modification of this tariff item, which will permit the rough stone to come in at precisely the. same rate of duty existing to-day, and give the work upon that rough stone, the sawing, the dressing and the planing to the stonecutters of Canada. We propose, therefore, that stone sawn on two-sides shall continue to come in at the present rate of duty but that on stone sawn on-four sides the rate shall be fifteen cents per 100 pounds. There is very great difficulty in administering the tariff to-day on account of the difficulty in ascertaining the value of finished, dressed stone coming in as an import. The average ad valorem of the specific rate which I have quoted is 30 per cent. Upon turned, planed, cut or further finished stone I propose a rate of 45 cents per 100 pounds, which is equal to 30 per cent ad valorem. The reason why that higher rate is about the equivalent ad valorem rate to the lower specific rate on stone sawn on four sides is because of the greater value of the stone which has been planed, turned, cut or further finished. These are the proposals which the Government has to offer in regard to building stone, and I believe that the increase in the tariff rate will enure directly to the benefit of the stonecutters of Canada and indirectly to the country.
One further item-caustic soda and hypochlorite of lime. At present these two items are on the free list. The Canadian Salt Company at Windsor, which employs many men and has a large capital invested in its plant, has for three years been manufacturing these products made from salt. The manufacture of caustic soda and hypochlorite of lime-which is a by-product of
24S4

- caustic soda-is a natural industry in connection with salt production. The users of caustic soda and chloride of lime are the soap and paper manufacturers, but they use a very small proportion indeed having regard to their production. Therefore, it is not necessary that there should be any readjustment or increase of the tariff by reason of the rates which I shall have the honour to propose to the House. The Canadian Salt Company at Windsor produce now one-third of Canada's requirements in caustic soda. They hope, with the aid of this duty, to produce all. Later, I shall give, in the resolutions which I shall propose, the rates of duties which I have to offer with respect to these two commodities.
I come now to another matter which has been brought to our attention; that is, the tariff with respect to brass. In the tariff of 1907 brass in sheets, bars and rods was dutiable at 10 per cent. It was not manufactured in Canada, and, under a provision of the Customs Act, on August 11, 1908, the Governor in Council abolished the duty of 10 per cent on brass bars and rods, and it consequently was placed upon the free list. I have stated that it -was not then manufactured in Canada. However, I am now glad to say that it is manufactured in Canada. A new plant, involving a capital of about $250,000, modern, up to date, and well equipped, has been established at West Toronto for the manufacture of copper and brass. I propose now, and it also will involve no tariff adjustment, to restore the item of brass in sheets, bars and rods to the tariff, fixing the same duty as was fixed with respect to it in the tariff of 1907.
Now, I approach the end of what I fear has been a somewhat long-drawn-out and tedious Budget. There are a number of minor changes, some of consequence, but chiefly for administrative purposes. Before reaching the resolutions which we have to propose, in order to give notice of them, there is a matter to which I desire briefly to advert and it is the question of a bounty upon iron ore. This matter has been brought to the attention of the Government by the hon. member for Thunder Bay and Eainy River (Mr. Carrick) who, in a very able speech, introduced the subject to the House. The matter has been discussed in the press, and I notice that it has been made the subject of a debate in
	-
the Legislature of the province of Ontario. Without dilating further upon the subject, because the debate which ensued was of a very illuminating and informing character, I desire to say that the Government feels that at the present time it has not sufficient information before it as a basis for intelligent legislative action. Speaking this afternoon with regard to the question of bounties generally, I said that, personally, I saw no objection to bounties granted for the purpose of calling an industry into being, but that there was a strong objection to continuing bounties to industries that had been firmly established. We propose, in respect to this important matter, which has been brought to our attention by the hon. member for Thunder Bay and Rainy River to cause an inquiry to be' instituted by the Mines Department during the qoming summer for the purpose of ascertaining the extent and availability of Canada's ore deposits and the character of the ore, and securing information as complete as possible as to improved methods of treatment. We desire to ascertain, as a result of that inquiry, whether a bounty will induce development and place the Canadian iron ore industry in a reasonable time upon a secure basis, enabling it to compete with foreign ore without the adventitious aid of further bounties.
There is another matter also involving the question of bounties which I desire to call to the attention of the House. There has been placed before us recently, in fact since the beginning of the year, the question of the development in Canada of flax fibre production. I think that the development of the industry of flax fibre production would be of great advantage to certain parts of Canada provided it could be-carried on successfully here. But the success of manufacturing flax fibre will depend upon the efficiency of the flax pulling machines and the flax fibre manufacturing machines. I am unable at present to express any opinion as to whether the flax fibre industry is one which, having regard to the labour conditions that prevail in this country, and the stage of invention of the machinery required, should	be	regarded	as	a possibleindustry, but during the summer it is our	intention	to	look fully
into the matter and see whether such an industry is possible of development in Canada, and whether a reasonable bounty

would have the effect of contributing to its institution and development.
By whom will the inquiry be made?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The first inquiry will be
made by the Mines Department, and I am now communicating with Mr. Brock. The second inquiry will be conducted by the officers of the Finance Department, tariff branch. That is what I have in my mind at the present time. If it is necessary, we can easily obtain outside expert assistance in the matter.
I propose to offer an amendment to section 7 of the Customs Tariff Act of 1907. That section is as follows:
Articles which are the produce or manufacture of any foreign country which treats imports from Canada less favourably than those from other countries may he subject to a surtax over and above the duties specified in schedule 'A' to this Act, such surtax in every case to he one-third of the duty specified in the general tariff in the said schedule.
I would call the attention of the House ' to the fact that the provision of one-third is inflexible; that is to say, it must be one-third, no more and no less. In similar legislation in other countries-Germany, Japan and Italy-there is a provision that the surtax may be a rate not exceeding 50 per cent or 30 per cent; that is to say, it is in the discretion of the Government whether it will be 2 per cent, or 15 per cent, or more.
I purpose, Sir, offering an amendment to section 7 of the customs tariff, which will provide that imports from countries which discriminate against the imports of Canada or against Canadian shipping may be subject to a surtax over and above the duty specified in the Customs Tariff Act, to an amount not exceeding twenty per cent ad valorem. That is to say, it may be two per cent, or five per cent, or ten per cent, or fifteen per cent, but it must not, under any circumstances, exceed twenty per cent, ad valorem. Mr. Speaker, this is the third occasion upon which I have had the honour of presenting the Budget to the House, and I have again to express my most grateful thanks for the courtesy, attention and patience with which you have heard me.

Mr. Speaker, during the day the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance were good enough to agree to the adjournment of the debate this evening until to-morrow, if we upon this side of the House so desired, and I wish to acknowledge their courtesy in that regard. It has come to my attention, however, that a great number of hon. gentlemen upon this side of the House desire that the debate Shall be resumed, not to-morrow, but after the Easter holidays, upon a date to be fixed by the Government. In any event, the debate cannot be concluded before the adjournment on Wednesday of this week, and I think it would be just as well if the debate were adjourned at this 'stage, as to-morrow or the following day. Further, a great number of the members of the House who live at a distance from Ottawa, will be leaving tomorrow, and I imagine that there will be a very small attendance in the House. I trust, therefore, the Prime Minister will agree that the debate be adjourned this evening, to be resumed on, say, Thursday of next week.
It was suggested to me by the hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) that, in the event of an adjournment this evening until next week, it would be but fair that the Prime Minister should be advised by the Opposition of any amendment contemplated to the resolution just moved by the Minister of Finance. I have conferred with the leader of the Opposition upon this point, and I am in a position to say that, in the event of such an adjournment being granted, he will be pleased to communicate the substance of any amendment which may be contemplated by the Opposition. 1 trust that my suggestion that the debate
be adjourned till Thursday of next week will be favourably received by the Govern ment.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think it would not be quite regular to move that the debate be adjourned to any specific date.
I would move the adjournment of the debate.

speechtext: I understand that it would not be very convenient for some hon. gentlemen on this side of the House who intend to speak immediately after my hon. friend (Mr. A. K. We will not ask my hon. friend to go on to-night, and we can discuss the other matter later.

I understand that Dr. Pinault, the former physician, was summarily dismissed. He is one of the most

He was physician in charge of these Indians, but was summarily dismissed without investigation or a chance to say a word in his behalf, and a new medical man was appointed but refused to accept the position. Dr. Price, I think, was the man who refused. It was then passed over to Dr. Martin. I do not know who the physician is now, but I understand that the position is very unsatisfactory and may cost the department more than under the old system.

speechtext: I understand that a sawmill firm wanted to secure a portion of the reserve for a planing mill, but the Indians have expressed their unwillingness to surrender.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The department have no
authority to take away any property of the Indians without their consent. My hon. friend is referring to the letter the chief of the Caughnawaga tribe wrote in connection with amendment to the Act made in 1911 by my predecessor. Where land is required for public purposes it is secured, if not provided for by the expropriation provisions of the Indian Act, through the agency of the Exchequer Court which holds an inquiry as to the expediency of the sale. It allots a counsel to the Indians, hears evidence and then refers the matter to the Governor in Council who in turn refers it to Parliament. Parliament has to pass upon the sale before the lands are disposed of.

speechtext:
I believe the medical man previously on that reserve was Dr. Mitchell.
I think his salary was $500. He has been succeeded by Dr. Wood, and I think his salary has been somewhat increased.
Is that the same Dr. Wood who was in charge of the patronage in West Middlesex?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No, I understand that Dr. Wood resigned any patronage that he may have had.
Can the minister inform me on that point?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No, I cannot.
I think it would be well for the Minister to look into that matter.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I know that he was informed by me that he would have to drop that part of the business.

If the minister will make inquiries he will find that Dr. Wood has been dispensing the patronage in that district in violation of the rule laid down by the Government that a public official shall not take part in politics. It will be found that he has been guilty, while being a servant of this Government, of being an active participant in political matters, and that therefore, according to the rule which has been laid down, he merits dismissal from his position. I do not think that the information the minister has given me is quite correct in regard to the doctor whom Dr. Wood succeeded. I would like to know why Dr. Dewar was dismissed and why Dr. Wood succeeded him and whether there is any difference in their remuneration?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I understand that there were two medical men previously-Dr. Mitchell and Dr. Dewar. There were a great many complaints in as to the unsatisfactory service they were rendering.
In writing?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I am not sure whether they were in writing or not, but I am inclined to think that some complaints were made to me personally in regard to them.
If they were in writing will the minister lay them on the table?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes. They were succeeded by Dr. Wood.
What is the difference in remuneration?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Dr. Wood is getting $150 more than his predecessors.
Will the minister kindly verify that for me?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes.
Is there any regulation which prevents an Indian agent himself supplying goods to the Indians and then charging them up to the Government?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The regulations of the
department do not permit an Indian agent to sell direct to the Indians himself, and to then be paid by the Government.
Either directly or indirectly?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes.

What was the complaint
against Dr. Dewar and Dr. Mitchell?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I think the change took
place when I was not in the country, but I remember there was a Dr. Mitchell in western Ontario against whom complaints were made of inattention to his duty, and that he seldom responded to a call when he was sent for. Unless there are two doctor Mitchells there, this is the one.
What about Dr. Dewar?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I have no recollection at all about his case.

Was it because Dr. Dewar
was just charged with being a Liberal?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I do not know anything
about that case at all.
How many superintendents of Indian agencies are there in Nova Scotia?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Mr. Boyd is the only one.
Are all the Indian agents practically under his jurisdiction?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: He has general supervision over all the agencies.
What repairs were done to the Indian council-house at Chapel Island in Richmond county, and what is the council-house used for?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The Indians for many
years past had a general council-house there, at which they met at least once a

year to hold a mission and
10 p.m. conduct their business. It was destroyed by fire, and they having no financial resources sufficient to build, we agreed, if they furnished the material, to supply them with skilled [DOT]labour, etc.
Are the medical attendants of the Indians paid a fixed salary, and is there something extra allowed them in *case of epidemics?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The medical attendant is paid a fixed salary for normal attendance, but if there is an epidemic, or if he has heavy operations to perform, which cause abnormal conditions, an extra allowance is sometimes made.
How much has Dr. Woods been paid since he was appointed by this Government as medical attendant to the Indians in Middlesex county?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I have not the information at hand.
Indians, N.S.-Belief and seed grain, $6,000.
What is this money used for?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The greater part of this expenditure is for the relief of aged Indians, repairs to houses, and so on. Very little of it i,s used for seed grain.
How is the seed grain distributed?

By the Indian agent, who recommends the distribution.
Indians, N.S.-To provide for the encouragement of agriculture, $1,000.
How much is paid the teacher at Whycocomagh to teach the Indians how to cultivate the land?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I cannot find from the Auditor-General's Report that we paid him anything for that service last year.

There is $1,000 for encouragement to agriculture and $1,500 for Indian agents, so that it wduld look as if the agents were the wards of the nation and not the Indians. If you are going to do anything serious towards encouraging the Indians to take an interest in farming, you will have to make a larger appropriation for the purpose than $1,000; you will have to give them implements in the first place. Tf you divide

$1,000 between the different agencies, it will amount to a very small sum for each. I think that vote should be increased.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Probably the Indians are so thrifty they do not require very much Government assistance in that line.
Perhaps the minister thinks that the reduction in agricultural implements promised in the Budget speech to-day will enable them to get along without an increased grant.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I have here a list of their increased crops-5,510 bushels of potatoes, 178 bushels turnips, 620 bushels oats, 40 bushels barley, 12J bushels corn, 35 bushels beans, 53 bushels apples. So they are doing very well.
Indians, Nova Scotia-Medical attendance-and medicines, $5,000.
Will the minister please give the names of the doctors and their salaries?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Drs. J. A. McDonald, Richmond, $250; Geo. McNally, King's West, $200; A. M. Hebb, Lunenburg East, $50; C. S. Marshall, Lunenburg West, $60; H. N. McDonald, Whycocomagh Reserve, Inverness, $175; J. G. Macauley, Malagawatch Reserve, Inverness, $100; Hector A. Grant, Victoria, $325; C. J. Sparrow, Cape Breton, $350; W. F. McKinnon, Antigonish, $250; C. H. Morris, Martook, Hants Co., $75; J. McKenzie, Pictou, $200; R. Withers, Le-quille, Annapolis, $50; J. A. Sponagle, Middleton, $50; H. V. Kent, Colchester, $150; E. O. Hallett, Weymouth, Digby county, $100; C. C. Archibald, Bear River, $250; T. R. Ford, Milton, Queens county, $100; W. H. Cole, Bridgewater, Lunenburg,
$50; -. 

, Parrsborough, Cumberland,
$200; A. Culton, Shubenacadie, Hants, $150; W. B. Moore, Kings East, $200.
Has any appointment been made in place of Dr. Millar, at Tusket in Yarmouth county? He resigned and went away?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I think Dr. Bethune was appointed in his place.
Is there any proposal to purchase any additional land in connection with the reserve at Pictou Landing?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No. I do not remember any such application.

In some places,
particularly in Antigonish county, there

are Indian reserves on which the hay is let year after year. I had a question on the Order Paper earlier in the session whether it was proposed to let the Indian reserve at Heatlierton. I think the answer was that the matter was under consideration. I desire to know whether the minister will call for tenders or whether the agent will have the privilege of farming it out as he has done before?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I understand this is a small affair, but it is proposed to ask for tenders.
Indians, Nova Scotia-Repairs to roads and dyking, $600.

Will the hon.
minister please state what amount is spent at the Indian reservation in Inverness county?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Malagawatch reserve,
$204.38; Middle River reserve, $1,999.93; Whycocomagh reserve, $101.61.
Can the minister give me the names of those who supervised the work?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The Auditor General's
Report does not contain the names, but I can get them if the hon. gentleman desires it.	.
At what date was Mr. Woods informed that he would have to ' drop his connection with patronage?.'

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I cannot remember the
date. But I remember that he wrote me that he was occupying a position with respect to party politics and asked my opinion as to his retaining it. I informed him that he must drop it, that no person occupying a position under the Government should have to do with party politics. And I understand he has followed that direction.

On the 8th of November, 1913, he wrote a letter asking that a certain postmaster be dismissed. So that in November last, Dr. Woods, while Indian medical attendant, was interested actively in politics, so actively that he was controlling the patronage in the district. If the minister wrote him to observe the rule against political partisanship and he did not observe that rule, I think that the minister should take means to enforce the law on the subject. Surely, the minister will see the propriety and necessity of such action.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
That was nearly five months ago, * and I am sure that it was since that date that I first learned of the position he 157
held. Of course, as soon as it was brought to my attention-and I could not act any sooner-I gave him his instructions, and I am confident he has lived up to those instructions since that time.
The minister will let me know if it was really before that date ?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes.
What provision has the minister made for the roads on the Whycocomagh reserve ?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: It is expected to spend $300 there.

There are two miles of road through this reservation and it is in very bad condition.
Indians, Nova Scotia-Rebuilding Indian council house, Chapel island, $2,500.
Will the minister advertise for tenders for this ?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: We frequently put up these buildings by means of Indian labour and do not find it necessary to call for tenders when only a small amount is involved. We will consider what particular form this should take, but perhaps the most economical way will be to use Indian labour.

Is this the first time
that the department has built a council house for the Indians in Nova Scotia?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Probably it is the first
time, but the council house was burned down and inasmuch as the Indians have no funds of their own they cannot rebuild for themselves.
The only building that was burned down there, to my knowledge, was an old church.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I understand that there is a church at the same place; it is called Burnt church. I do not know whether or not it is utilized for church purposes.

If this vote is for the purpose of rebuilding the Indian chapel on Chapel island, the amount is not too large, but if it is for the building of an ordinary council house I think $2,500 is a rather large amount. You can build a magnificent residence in that part of the country for $2,500.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The whole of this amount may not necessarily be expended.
Inlians, New Brunswick-Repairs to roads, $450.
Air. A1ICHAUD: A piece of road called the main road runs along the Indian reser-



vation in the county in which I live, for a distance of a mile or a mile and a half. I would call the attention of the minister to the fact that the money which is voted comes along in the month of July or August when it is practically too late to be of any real benefit. If we could get it in May or early in June so that it could be spent in the early part of the season it would be of much greater benefit.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Of what reserve is the hon. gentleman speaking?

The Edmonton reserve. We get money from the department every second year, as a rule; we should have it every year. The municipalities spend a certain amount of money on this road, but we can get no assistance from the province, and early in the spring and well into the summer the road is usually in a very bad condition.
Indians, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and Northwest Territories-Dive stock, $9,480.
What is this item for?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Pure bred livestock.

On the Peigan reserve during the last two or three years a large number of the mares and stallions belonging to the Indians have been destroyed because of their having contagious diseases, and compensation has been paid by the Government. Does that money pass into the hands of the Indians, or into the hands of the Indian agent in trust?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: It is paid to the Indians through the agent.

Some of these animals are owned by the Indians, and others are owned by the department. In the case of their being owned by the department, I presume the money compensation made in such instances is reinvested in stallions for the use of the Indian reserve?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The Indians have the privilege of utilizing this money in any way they choose, and they can utilize it by reinvesting it, if they so desire, in the purchase of other animals..
But not necessarily?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
No.
Indians, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and Northwest Territories.-Supplies for destitute Indians, $142,148.

This is a large item;
will the minister give the committee .some explanation ?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The amount for Manitoba
is $33,062; for Saskatchewan. $109,086 and for Alberta $104,000.

What is a destitute
Indian?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
One, who, by reason of
physical disability or other cause, is unable to provide for himself and must be cared for by tho department.
Indians, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, and Northwest Territories-Hospitals, medical attendance, etc., $104,042.

Are these hospitals on
the Indian reserves?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Where there are Indian
hospitals they are located on reserves, bu|t some Indians are committed to other hospitals and we have to pay for attendance.

* I see by the Auditor's Report itemls of six hundred pounds of tea supplied by H. N. Bate and Sons of Ottawa for the Duck Lake agency in Saskatchewan and blankets supplied by G. M. Garland and Son of Ottawa. Then Green-shields of Montreal supply goods there. Is there not some mistake or why are these goods purchased at such a distance from the reserve?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
These are all purchased
by tender and these are the lowest tenderers. When they are .purchased in the East they are delivered in Winnipeg where we have a warehouse, and we pay the freight from there to the reserves.
Indians, British Columbia*-Travelling expenses, $16,000.
Would the minister explain this?

We have a number of
agents in British Columbia who travel a good deal inspecting. Then there is a good deal of travelling in connection with the maintenance of law and order, the prevention of intoxicants., etc. The distances in British Columbia are greater than in the other provinces and the travelling expenses arc heavier.

I understand that the
agent at the Hobbema reserve, Mr. Mann, was relieved of his office. He had been in the service thirty-five years, his health had broken down and I understood the department intended to show some special consideration to him.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Mr. Mann is a very old
official and has been retained in an advisory capacity at a salary of some $600.

That is all right.
Indians, British Columbia-Surveys, $10,000.
What is meant by surveys?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The surveying of Indian reserves.
Indian education, $948,115.
Who is the Indian teacher at Malagawateh reserve, Nova Scotia?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I am not able to give the information just at the moment. I understand the school is closed at the present time.

Was there a
teacher there last season?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I can get the information for my horn, friend later on.
I will come to the rescue of the minister. My information is that a young Indian teaches there and I would like to know whether he has the necessary qualications.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I will get the information.

I would like to refer to a matter that has been brought up in this House before. I refer to the teacher at St. Peter's. Provincial inspector of schools, Mr. T. J. McNeil, refused to visit or have anything to do with the school on the ground that the teacher was not qualified. This young man was appointed after Miss Devereaux's dismissal and I would like to know whether he has the necessary qualifications now.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I cannot tell the hon. member.

It is a rather peculiar state of affairs if we are to pass estimjates for Indian education all over the country without being in a position to know whether the teachers are qualified. I think the minister should be in a position to tell me whether licensed teachers or backwoodsmen are teaching the children in the province of Nova Scotia in which I am interested.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I understand that no
teacher is employed in any school unless he is properly qualified.

Last year it was proved to the hilt in this House that the young
man succeeding Miss Devereaux was not qualified under the Provincial Education A>ct of Nova Scotia.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I 'have a hazy recollection of having read the papers in connection with that and of the discussion that took place. I understand that Miss Devereaux was dismissed for very strong reasons, opening school after ten o'clock in the morning-

I am not finding fault with her dismissal, but with the fact that the person appointed in her stead was not qualified. The provincial inspector of schools refused to visit the school on that account. Has the department seen to it that that school has now a qualified teacher ?

I think the minister will find he has something to attend to with respect to the qualification of teachers for Indian schools. It is all very well to say that a teacher is qualified because somebody else says so, but there are certain qualifications required by the Provincial Education Acts, and the minister cannot hope to have Indian schools in their proper condition unless he sees that every teacher possesses the recognized qualifications. I cannot understand how this Malagawateh teacher can have the qualifications. I had the opportunity of recommending a couple of men myself as teachers at Indian schools, but I took very great care that the persons I recommended were qualified under the provincial law.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I understand that teachers are appointed on the recommendation of the Indian agents and inspectors. Personally, I am not aware of any complaints having been made to the department with regard to the qualifications of those teachers, except the case that came up last year, and I am not sure whether that particular teacher is still employed. Perhaps he is better qualified by this time. It is not so very unusual a thing to have an Indian teacher.

I quite recognize that. I am not reflecting on his appointment because he is an Indian, but I know this man very well, and I can hardly see how he could possess the qualifications. That is just the point. Men are sent out to teach without the necessary license. It is quite possible that that may be done successfully in some cases, but it is opening the door to a very dangerous practice.
It is quite possible that politics may enter into this thing and that an inspector may

be induced to recommend a person who lias not the necessary qualifications, but if that practice is to be followed there will be a great deal of trouble.
We have adopted a rule to have qualified teachers wherever possible, but in some cases we are not able to get qualified teachers for Indian schools, then we get the best qualified person we can.
How is this money distributed between the provinces ?

Ontario, $126,825; Quebec, $12,040; Nova Scotia, $5,125; New Brunswick, $6,525; Prince Edward Island, $400; Manitoba, $249,280; Saskatchewan, $157,095;-Alberta, $138,175; Northwest Territories, $18,100; British Columbia, $216,800; Yukon, $9,750; generally, $8,000.
How many teachers are employed on the staff, and what grades do they teach?
There are 249 day schools, 58 boarding schools, and 19 industrial schools, or a total of 326.
Has industrial school education proved satisfactory?
In some places very satisfactory.
It is a most expensive system of education, is it not?
It is a somewhat expensive method, but it is very useful in teaching the Indians to better their position and to fit them for various occupations.

The school at Elkhorn appears to be doing good work. If more of that type of school were established, you could probably do away with some of these day schools. The industrial schools might require more highly paid teachers because they have to be specialists in their way. The boys are fitted for work that will bring them good wages if they wish to follow any particular occupation, and the girls are taught sewing and house work.
Elkhorn is the model of all the industrial schools.
Would the minister get me the information I asked for in reference to the teacher at St. Peter's? Personally, I have no interest in the matter, but I have been asked to mention it to the minister.

I have made a note of it.

Indians-A. J. Boyd, inspector of Maritime provinces, $1,600; timber inspector and valuator, $1,200.
What are the duties of the timber inspector?

A. J. Boyd is the name of the inspector, and he is the superintendent for New Brunswick and the other Maritime provinces. He has charge of all the agencies. The timber inspector and valuator is Mr. George Shaw, of Thessalon, and he receives $1,200. There are about 400 lots unsurrendered and unsold in the Indian lands on the north shore of Lake Huron, and Mr. Shaw's duty is to value the timber on the lots disposed of.
Payment to Indians surrendering their lands, under provisions of section 70, of the Indian Act, which will afterwards be repaid from the avails of the land, $50,000.
What lands are referred to there?	[DOT]
When we ask the surrender of any land under the Indian Act, the Indians are entitled to fifty per cent of the proceeds of the sale, and this is the appropriation out of which that amount is paid.
Could the minister tell me whether any lands will be sold in Alberta this coming year?
There have been some surrenders near Calgary, on the Sarcee, but we have not decided as to when the sale shall take place.
What is the estimate by which the minister arrives at $50,000.
This is the item which ha3 been voted year after year.
Do I understand that this is a fund to be at hand when it is wanted for - the purpose of paying for Indian lands that are sold.

It is for the purpose of
advancing cash payments to the Indians at the time of surrender.
Relief to destitute Indians in remote districts, $35,000.

What do you call
remote districts?

In the northern territories, such as Ungava and the Mackenzie Basin.
Indians-To prevent spread of tuberculosis,
What is being done to prevent the spread of tuberculosis?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
This vote is to provide
hospital treatment for those who can avail themselves of it, methods of sanitation, the destruction of infected houses and the re-building of others to combat the spread of the disease. Wq intend to give rather more attention to this phase of the work in future than we have in the past. We have had a number of complaints that tuberculosis is very prevalent on some of the reserves, and we are endeavouring to teach the Indians the necessity for sanitation with a view of stamping out this disease.
Is tuberculosis supposed to be decreasing among the Indians? We are told that the Indians are peculiarly the victims of this disease.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: It has not decreased, I am sorry to say.
While the population is increasing.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Very little.
Grant to assist Indian Trust Fund Account $310-Suppression of liquor, $6,000.
What is this for?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: This is intended to assist the Indian Trust Fund, which receives credit of a moiety of the fines imposed and bears the expenditure of preventive, detective and police service in carrying out the law. and in preventing the illegal sale of liquor to the Indians.
Is anything done by the department to prevent the sale of liquor to Indians in the Maritime provinces?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The officials of the reserves attend to that.
Who looks after that in the city of Sydney?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The agent resides close to the reserve there.

I would not blame the
agent for not spending very much of his time endeavouring to detect those who sell liquor to the Indians. The situation in Sydney is peculiar. We are supposed to have prohibition, but, as a matter of fact, liquor is sold very openly, and unfortunately it is sold quite freely to the Indians. It is not a rare occurrence to see an Indian woman going around our streets drunk. Of course, the medical officer of the reserve cannot attend to that, but in a place like Sydney with a population of 20,000 and a large Indian
reservation nearby, I should think the department ought to pay some small salary to, say a police officer, to take a special interest in that particular phase of the Indian question. The Indians, unfortunately, become very fond of intoxicating liquor and are seriously injured in every way through its use. On the Malagawatch and Whycoeomagh reserves the danger is not so great because there is not such opportunity for the Indians on these reserves to obtain whisky. Those who sell liquor to Indians at Sydney are occasionally prosecuted, but the trouble is to find any officers who will take a special interest in enforcing the law.
Progress reported.
On motion of Mr. Rogers, the House adjourned at 11 p.m.
Tuesday, April 7, 1914.
